content: Pertussis, commonly referred to as whooping cough, is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis. This organism is a Gram-negative, aerobic, non-motile coccobacillus. The disease primarily spreads through direct contact with aerosolized respiratory droplets from infected individuals. The risk factors for developing pertussis include lack of vaccination or incomplete vaccination, exposure to infected individuals, being an infant or child under the age of 5, and having an immunocompromised status. Infants younger than 12 months who are unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated are at the highest risk for severe infection, life-threatening complications, and death. The clinical course of pertussis is divided into three stages: the catarrhal stage, the paroxysmal stage, and the convalescent stage. If untreated, patients typically experience low-grade fever, coryza (runny nose, occasional cough), and mild symptoms during the catarrhal stage, which lasts 1–2 weeks. This is followed by the paroxysmal stage, characterized by violent coughing fits with a distinctive whooping sound during inspiration, lasting 1–6 weeks. Recovery occurs during the convalescent stage. Adolescents and adults often have a milder disease course, and the characteristic whooping cough may be absent. Complications of pertussis include apnea, pneumonia, otitis media, pneumothorax, refractory pulmonary hypertension, seizures, and, in severe cases, death. Prognosis is generally excellent, but severe complications are more common in unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated infants under 12 months of age. The diagnosis of pertussis is typically based on clinical findings and confirmed through laboratory tests such as nasopharyngeal culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), or serology. Nasopharyngeal culture is considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Chest radiography is usually unremarkable but may show findings such as atelectasis or lymphadenopathy in some cases. Treatment of pertussis involves antibiotic therapy, with macrolides (e.g., azithromycin, clarithromycin) being the first-line agents. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate macrolides. Early treatment is critical, particularly for infants under 1 year of age and pregnant women near term, as it reduces disease severity and transmission. Antibiotics are most effective when initiated within three weeks of cough onset in individuals older than 1 year and within six weeks for infants and pregnant women. Vaccination is the primary method of preventing pertussis. The DTaP vaccine is recommended in a series of five doses during childhood, with a booster dose (Tdap) during adolescence or adulthood. The Tdap vaccine contains lower concentrations of diphtheria and pertussis toxoids compared to the DTaP vaccine. Post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics may be recommended for high-risk individuals to prevent disease development or complications. Patients who have previously been infected with pertussis or vaccinated against it may still be reinfected, but subsequent infections are typically milder. Secondary prevention measures include post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis for individuals at high risk of severe disease or complications. Prophylactic regimens are similar to those used for treatment and vary based on the individual’s age. Historically, pertussis was first described in the 12th century, with outbreaks documented in Persia in 1502 and France in 1578. Bordetella pertussis was isolated in 1906 by Jules Bordet and Octave Gengou, who also developed the first vaccine and serological test for the disease. In the 1940s, the first combination DTP vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) was developed. Due to adverse effects associated with the whole-cell DTP vaccine, a safer acellular DTaP vaccine was introduced in Japan in 1981. The pathophysiology of pertussis is primarily toxin-mediated. Bordetella pertussis attaches to the cilia of respiratory epithelial cells, proliferates, and produces virulence factors that paralyze the cilia and cause inflammation of the respiratory tract. This interferes with the clearance of pulmonary secretions. Virulence factors include pertussis toxin (PT), filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA), fimbriae (FIM), adenylate cyclase toxin (ACT), tracheal cytotoxin (TCT), lipooligosaccharide (LOS), and dermonecrotic toxin (DNT). These factors enable the bacterium to attach, proliferate, and evade the host immune system. Differential diagnosis of pertussis includes other causes of cough, dyspnea, and coryza, such as asthma, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, croup, the common cold, cystic fibrosis, foreign body aspiration, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and sinusitis. The incidence of pertussis is thought to be increasing due to declining vaccination rates and diminished herd immunity. Infants and young children under 5 years of age are more commonly affected than adults, and there is no gender predilection. Pertussis-related deaths are rare but more common in developing countries, among infants under 6 months of age, and in adults with significant comorbidities.
